title: Tazria: the priest must look (Leviticus 13:2–3)
hook: the priest examines in person, never from a distance

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzara'at, which the rabbis read as harmful speech made visible. Your line was words show on the skin. Today, who decides.

A rumor reaches you: so-and-so has really changed, and not for the better. You haven't seen them in a year. You've heard it from two people, maybe three, and by dinner it's easy to half believe it. Leviticus thirteen imagines a camp where a mark appears on someone's skin. Everyone can see it. Neighbors could whisper; family could guess. But the text gives the call to exactly one person, and it gives that person one instruction before anything else.
screen: `A RUMOR REACHES YOU.` → `EVERYONE CAN SEE THE MARK.` → `ONE INSTRUCTION FIRST.`

segments.voice: Start with where the person goes. When someone has a rising, a scab or a bright spot on the skin, they are brought to Aaron the priest or one of his sons. Not to the neighbors, not to the group, but to someone whose job is to look carefully. Then the priest looks. The Hebrew verb ra'ah, to see, comes again and again in this chapter. Has the hair in the spot turned white? Does it seem deeper than the skin? Only after looking does he say a word. No ruling from across the camp, no verdict by report. The looking has rules, too. The Mishnah says the priest doesn't examine in the early morning or the evening, or indoors, or on a cloudy day, because in poor light a dull spot can look bright; and not at noon, when a bright one can look dull. Even good eyes need good light. And nobody judges their own. The Mishnah also says a person may examine anyone's affliction except his own, and one opinion adds: or a close relative's. People are bad judges of what's too close to them. Put together, it's a whole ethic of looking: come close, look yourself, wait for the right light, and step aside when you can't see straight. Some teachers carry it far beyond skin, to every time someone is tempted to decide about a person from a distance.
screen: `BROUGHT TO THE PRIEST.` · `RA'AH: THE PRIEST MUST SEE.` · `NOT AT DUSK, NOT ON A CLOUDY DAY.` · `NO ONE EXAMINES THEIR OWN.` · then, large: `LOOK, DON'T ASSUME.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've formed an opinion about from a distance: from a story, a post, a single bad moment. Ask yourself the priest's questions: have I actually seen this, or only heard it; am I looking in good light, or when I'm tired and annoyed; am I too close to judge fairly? Then hold your opinion a little more loosely, until you can look again.
Tazria. The portion where the priest must come close and look for himself, in good light, before he says anything at all.
Your line: look, don't assume. Good light and a close look come before any verdict. That's day three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on judging others draws on Pirkei Avot's advice to judge every person favorably and not to judge another until you stand in their place, and some teachers pair Tazria with it.

chat.says: In Leviticus, who decides whether a mark on someone's skin is serious?
options: A priest, who must come close and look himself, in good light, before saying anything.
The neighbors, since everyone in the camp could see the mark for themselves.
The person, who checks their own skin and reports what they find to the camp.
chat.meaning: The person is brought to the priest, who must look for himself, in good light. The Mishnah adds that no one examines their own affliction.

ra'ah.meaning: to see; the verb this chapter keeps repeating

Aaron.meaning: Moses' brother; he and his sons examined the marks

Mishnah.meaning: the early rabbis' collection of Jewish law and teaching

Tazria.meaning: when a woman conceives; this portion's name

notes: Mishnah Negaim 2:2 lighting rules (not early morning, evening, indoors, cloudy day; not noon) cited from memory; confirm.
Negaim 2:5: 'all afflictions a person may examine except his own'; Rabbi Meir adds relatives. Confirm attribution.
'Dozens of times' for forms of ra'ah in Lev 13: a count wasn't made; confirm or soften.
Negaim 3:1 (a non-priest expert may examine but only a priest declares) is not mentioned, to keep the day simple.
